reason: The recovery tube's picture shows useful substances moving from the tube back toward blood.

effect: Useful substances and much water have returned to the blood; the remaining fluid still needs a route to the bladder.
reaction: It makes sense now why filtering alone would not be enough.
reason: The ureters are shown leading from the kidneys toward the bladder, so they should start the drainage route.

effect: The ureters now connect to the kidney outlets; the bladder still needs attaching.
reason: The bladder is the remaining named slot and receives the ureters.
expectation: The bladder should attach to the ureters, completing the route from the kidneys.

effect: The kidneys now have a continuous route through the ureters to the bladder; the remaining fluid still needs to be collected.
reaction: The completed route is easy to follow.
reason: The fluid left after recovery contains waste, and the completed kidney pair provides the route to the bladder.
expectation: The remaining fluid should travel through the ureters and collect in the bladder as urine.

effect: The remaining fluid reached the bladder as urine, completing both the recovery and drainage goals.
reaction: The separate blood and urine routes make the finished model easy to follow.

mostWorthwhile.text: Filtering the blood and then recovering useful substances was most worthwhile: it showed why the kidney does more than simply remove waste.

leastWorthwhile.text: Attaching the ureters and bladder was clear but less engaging because the named slots made the sequence predictable.

surprise.text: I was surprised that glucose and other useful substances pass through the filter and must be taken back.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures and goals explained the pairings.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: seeing how the filter and recovery tube work together made me curious about how another body system fits together.
